newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu heads home as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu heads home as rebels advance.

text.p: Zaire's ailing and embattled president, Mobutu Sese Seko, left France for home on Friday after pleading for national unity in the face of growing popular support for rebels led by Laurent Kabila.
Mobutu, who left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment, called for a truce and a national council to find a peace settlement.

"At a time when I am preparing to return to my country to find myself again among my people, I invite all Zaireans to rise (and stand) together," Mobutu said in a hand-written statement issued from his villa in the south of France.

Much depended on the response of Kabila, whose Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) is advancing relentlessly across Zaire. He says only face-to-face talks with Mobutu will halt the fighting.
France and the United States made contingency plans to evacuate their nationals from Zaire if the need arose. France has sent troops and planes to nearby Gabon and Congo.

Mobutu left Nice airport on a private jet shortly after 9.45 a.m. (0845 GMT) -- one hour and 45 minutes after his scheduled departure time. Aides said on Thursday that he had been expected to arrive in Kinshasa around 3 p.m. (1400 GMT).
Mobutu's son, Nzanga, said in France on Thursday that his father no longer ruled out talks with rebel leaders but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament.
"His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command," he said.

Mobutu, 66, has spent most of his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mixture of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.
State television said on Thursday he would land in Kinshasa "ready to take up his responsibilities at an institutional level in the face of the current situation in the east".
Mobutu presented his proposed national council as a formula to find "appropriate ways" out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute about Zairean nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, who form the core of Kabila's fighting force. An alliance of anti-Mobutu groups rallied around the cause.
Kabila's popularity surged as his forces notched up victory after victory. Residents of Kinshasa's poor districts openly welcome the prospect of his arrival in the capital.
The rebel advance has fuelled fresh political squabbling within Zaire's political family as rivals keen not to lose out in any deal with Kabila jockey for position.

Zaire's main opposition group, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) of veteran radical Etienne Tshisekedi, said it shared Kabila's aim of toppling Mobutu and had sent envoys to talk to him.

Party general secretary Adrien Phongo said Mobutu had to endorse Tshisekedi as prime minister after the transitional parliament voted to sack Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who has come under fire for his handling of the war.
Supporters of Kengo, who says he will remain in the job until further notice, and of Mobutu say the vote was invalid.
